key_findings.finding: Immediate management is ABC resuscitation: secure the airway, provide assisted ventilation/oxygenation for shallow or inadequate respirations, support circulation with IV fluids and vasopressors if needed, correct hypothermia, monitor ECG/glucose/electrolytes, and admit to intensive care. There is no routine specific antidote for barbiturates.

source_tools.relevance: Critical-poisoning review emphasizes rapid supportive care and judicious antidote use

key_findings.finding: Assisted ventilation is clearly indicated in this comatose patient with shallow respirations. Urinary alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate can be considered for significant phenobarbital poisoning because phenobarbital is a weak acid and renal elimination can be enhanced at urine pH above about 7.5, but it is an adjunct—not a substitute for airway and ventilatory support—and evidence is limited; multiple-dose activated charcoal has shown greater phenobarbital clearance than urinary alkalinization alone in one clinical study.

source_tools.relevance: 2024 case demonstrates urinary alkalinization titrated to urine pH >7.5 in severe phenobarbital overdose
Comparative clinical study reports greater phenobarbital clearance with multiple-dose activated charcoal than urinary alkalinization alone

key_findings.finding: Comparison of interventions: single-dose activated charcoal is reasonable early only after the airway is protected; multiple-dose charcoal is particularly relevant for phenobarbital because it can enhance elimination. Gastric lavage is not routine and is reserved for exceptional, very early life-threatening ingestion with a protected airway. Naloxone is appropriate only if opioid co-ingestion is suspected; flumazenil is not indicated for barbiturate poisoning and may precipitate seizures or withdrawal; sodium bicarbonate is used for urinary alkalinization or for documented sodium-channel-blocker cardiotoxicity, not as a universal barbiturate antidote. Hemodialysis/hemoperfusion may be considered in massive or refractory phenobarbital poisoning with persistent coma, respiratory failure, shock, or inability to clear the drug, while supportive care remains the foundation.

source_tools.relevance: Critical-poisoning review supports judicious, indication-based use of charcoal and gastric lavage rather than routine decontamination or indiscriminate antidotes
